messages.content: Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6.

function.name: statistics_calculate_p_value
function.description: Calculate the p-value for a t-test on a single sample from a population. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_mean.description: The mean of the sample data. This is a float type value.

population_mean.description: The mean of the population data. This is a float type value.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample data. This is a float type value.

sample_size.description: The size of the sample data.

two_tailed.description: Whether the test is two-tailed. If not provided, default is true.

message.content:
**Standard error (standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean)**  

\[
SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.4}{\sqrt{40}}
     \approx \frac{1.4}{6.3249}
     \approx 0.2215
\]

So the standard deviation of the null‑hypothesis test (i.e., the standard error of the sample mean) is **≈ 0.22**.
message.reasoning:
The user says: "Calculate the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test with a sample mean of 98.2, standard deviation of 1.4, and sample size of 40 for a population mean of 98.6."

They want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? That likely means the standard error of the mean under the null hypothesis? Actually, they might want the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample mean under the null hypothesis. That would be sigma/sqrt(n). But we don't know population sigma; we have sample standard deviation 1.4. Usually we use sample standard deviation as estimate of population standard deviation. So standard error = sample_std_dev / sqrt(sample_size) = 1.4 / sqrt(40). Let's compute: sqrt(40) ≈ 6.3249. 1.4 / 6.3249 ≈ 0.2215. So about 0.2215.

But maybe they want the standard deviation of the null hypothesis test? They might want the standard deviation of the test statistic? For a t-test, the standard deviation of the t-statistic is sqrt((n-1)/n)? Actually, the t-statistic has a t-distribution with df = n-1. Its standard deviation is sqrt(df/(df-2)) if df > 2. For df=39, std dev = sqrt(39/37) ≈ sqrt(1.05405) ≈ 1.0268. But that's the standard deviation of the t distribution. It might be ambiguous. But likely they want the standard error of the mean: sqrt((s^2)/n). So answer: 0.2215.
